title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: LSASS Driver
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: LSASS Driver
summary: An LSASS driver is a library or driver-level component that the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service loads inside its own protected process, and adversaries abuse it for persistence that sits alongside credential material. Either a legitimate driver is replaced with a tampered copy, or an illegitimate one is registered so LSA operations load it. Because the substitute runs in the same process that authenticates users, it executes on every boot and every relevant security operation, and it can observe authentication data. The distinguishing artefacts are an unexpected module loaded into lsass.exe, a system file whose signature, size, or hash no longer matches the vendor baseline, and driver or service registration data that does not correspond to a known product. Defenders treat signature validation, hash comparison against a known-good set, and file integrity monitoring of the security subsystem components as the primary evidence, and they interpret a missing signature or a vendor mismatch as a stronger signal than an unfamiliar file name.

beginner.definition: LSASS is the Windows process that checks who you are when you sign in. It uses small helper files, called drivers or libraries, that sit inside it. An attacker can replace one of those helpers, or add a new one, so their code runs inside that protected process.
beginner.whyItMatters: That process handles the secrets used for sign-in. Code running inside it can watch those secrets and starts again at every boot. Because the helper file carries a trusted name, many checks pass it without a thought. This makes it a quiet way to stay on a computer and a serious risk to the accounts that use it.
howItWorks: Windows loads helper libraries and drivers into the LSASS process when the system starts.
These components handle parts of authentication and security policy for the computer.
An attacker replaces one of those files with a modified copy, or registers an extra one.
The next time the system starts, LSASS loads the attacker's file inside its own process.
The file then runs with the same protection that LSASS already has, and it can read authentication data.
Detection compares signatures and file hashes with the vendor originals rather than trusting file names.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital ward where the night desk checks every badge before letting anyone into the medicine room. Each desk drawer holds a printed procedure folder. Someone swaps one folder for an identical-looking copy that still shows the correct badge checks, but also quietly notes every PIN typed at the door.
takeaways: Verify the signature and hash of security subsystem components instead of trusting familiar file names.
Watch for unexpected libraries or drivers appearing inside the process that handles sign-in.
Legitimate updates change these files rarely, so record what is normal and review every deviation.

objectives: Explain what LSASS is and why it loads helper libraries and drivers.
Describe how an attacker replaces or adds a component so code runs inside the LSASS process at boot.
Identify the artefacts that reveal an altered driver, including signature and hash mismatches.
Detect unexpected software loaded into the LSASS process using integrity monitoring and baseline data.
Distinguish a legitimate driver update from an attacker modification.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from registering a security support provider.
